{"title": "Marts: Business-defined entities", "id": "4-marts", "info": "Our guidance here diverges if you use the dbt Semantic Layer. In a project without the Semantic Layer we recommend you denormalize heavily, per the best practices below. On the other hand, if you're using the Semantic Layer, we want to stay as normalized as possible to allow MetricFlow the most flexibility. Guidance for marts in a Semantic Layer context is on the next page.", "description": "This is the layer where everything comes together and we start to arrange all of our atoms (staging models) and molecules (intermediate models) into full-fledged cells that have identity and purpose. We sometimes like to call this the _entity_ _layer_ or _concept layer_, to emphasize that all our marts are meant to represent a specific entity or concept at its unique grain. For instance, an order, a customer, a territory, a click event, a payment — each of these would be represented with a distinct mart, and each row would represent a discrete instance of these concepts. Unlike in a traditional Kimball star schema though, in modern data warehousing — where storage is cheap and compute is expensive — we’ll happily borrow and add any and all data from other concepts that are relevant to answering questions about the mart’s core entity. Building the same data in multiple places, as we do with `orders` in our `customers` mart example below, is more efficient in this paradigm than repeatedly rejoining these concepts (this is a basic definition of denormalization in this context). Let’s take a look at how we approach this first layer intended expressly for exposure to end users.", "fileStructure": "models/marts
├── finance
│   ├── _finance_models.yml
│   ├── orders.sql
│   └── payments.sql
└── marketing
    ├── _marketing_models.yml
    └── customers.sql", "bestPractices": {"groupBy": "Group by department or area of concern. If you have fewer than 10 or so marts you may not have much need for subfolders, so as with the intermediate layer, don’t over-optimize too early. If you do find yourself needing to insert more structure and grouping though, use useful business concepts here. In our marts layer, we’re no longer worried about source-conformed data, so grouping by departments (marketing, finance, etc.) is the most common structure at this stage.", "nameBy": "Name by entity. Use plain English to name the file based on the concept that forms the grain of the mart `customers`, `orders`. Note that for pure marts, there should not be a time dimension (`orders_per_day`) here, that is typically best captured via metrics.", "avoid": "Build the same concept differently for different teams. `finance_orders` and `marketing_orders` is typically considered an anti-pattern. There are, as always, exceptions — a common pattern we see is that, finance may have specific needs, for example reporting revenue to the government in a way that diverges from how the company as a whole measures revenue day-to-day. Just make sure that these are clearly designed and understandable as _separate_ concepts, not departmental views on the same concept: `tax_revenue` and `revenue` not `finance_revenue` and `marketing_revenue`."}, "examples": [{"scenario": "A data analyst is working on a dbt project that requires connecting to a Snowflake database. They need to ensure that the connection settings are correctly configured to access the appropriate warehouse and database for their development environment.", "question": "Which settings should the analyst check in the `profiles.yml` file to confirm the correct configuration for connecting to Snowflake?", "options": ["The `target.warehouse` and `target.database` values in the `profiles.yml` file to ensure they are pointing to the correct warehouse and database.", "The `target.schema` and `target.threads` values in the `profiles.yml` file to confirm the correct schema and parallel execution settings.", "The `target.host` and `target.port` values in the `profiles.yml` file to validate the connection endpoint for Snowflake are valid and active.", "The `target.user` and `target.role` values in the `profiles.yml` file to verify the user credentials and role permissions for Snowflake have been set correctly."], "answer": "A", "explanation": "To confirm the correct connection settings for Snowflake in dbt, the analyst should verify the `target.warehouse` and `target.database` values in the `profiles.yml` file. These settings specify which warehouse and database the dbt models will be executed against. While the other settings (schema, threads, host, port, user, role) are important for other aspects of configuration, they do not directly address the warehouse and database connection, which is critical for ensuring the correct environment is used."}, {"scenario": "A data analyst is working on a project using dbt and needs to ensure that all models are built in a specific database called `sales_data`. The project is currently using the default `jaffle_shop` configuration, but the analyst wants to override the database setting for all models in the project to ensure they are built in the `sales_data` database.", "question": "How should the analyst modify the `dbt_project.yml` file to ensure all models are built into the `sales_data` database?", "options": ["Set the `database` key in the `dbt_project.yml` file to `sales_data`, applying the change globally across all models.", "Leave the `dbt_project.yml` file unchanged and manually define the `database` key in each model’s configuration file.", "Use the `generate_database_name` macro within the `dbt_project.yml` file to dynamically assign `sales_data` to each model.", "Modify the `project` key in the `dbt_project.yml` file to specify `sales_data` as the target database."], "answer": "A", "explanation": "To ensure that all models are built into the `sales_data` database, the correct approach is to set the `database` configuration in the `dbt_project.yml` file. This applies the setting globally, overriding the default `jaffle_shop` configuration for all models. Manually setting the database in each model would be inefficient. Using the `generate_database_name` macro is unnecessary for this task, and modifying the `project` key is incorrect, as it doesn't control the database setting."}, {"scenario": "A data analyst is working on a dbt project and needs to ensure that their database connection is functioning properly before continuing with development. They also want to verify the validity of their project configuration and check for any missing dependencies.", "question": "Which command should the analyst use to test the database connection and display relevant debugging information?", "options": ["`dbt debug` to test the connection, validate the project file, and check for missing dependencies.", "`dbt debug --connection` to only test the database connection without additional configuration checks.", "`dbt debug --config-dir` to locate the `profiles.yml` file and test the configuration settings.", "`dbt run --debug` to execute the models with detailed output but not specifically test the connection."], "answer": "C", "explanation": "The correct command is `dbt debug`, which not only tests the database connection but also checks for any issues in the project configuration and identifies missing dependencies. The command `dbt debug --connection` only tests the connection and skips additional checks, while `dbt debug --config-dir` only locates the `profiles.yml` file. The command `dbt run --debug` is used for running models with increased verbosity but does not serve as a connection test."}]}
